result:
Honest answer: I'd shrink the distance discount.

Right now, how much someone's suffering matters to us falls off steeply with distance—geographic, temporal, tribal, species. A child drowning in front of you commands everything; a child dying of something preventable four thousand miles away commands a shrug, not because anyone decided she matters less, but because caring just doesn't reach that far in the average human nervous system. Same with people who'll be alive in 200 years. Same with animals. The moral circle isn't small because people are bad; it's small because attention and empathy have a range, and most of the world's fixable misery sits just outside it.

If I could change one thing, I'd flatten that curve. Not eliminate it—you probably need some gradient to function, to love your own kids more than a stranger's—but make far-away suffering land with, say, a third of the weight of nearby suffering instead of a thousandth. I think an enormous amount would follow from that on its own: war, factory farming, climate procrastination, the tolerance of extreme poverty when the resources plainly exist. Those aren't really knowledge problems anymore. They're problems of things not mattering enough at the point where decisions get made.

Why that rather than "end suffering" or "cure disease"? Partly because those feel like wishes rather than changes—outcomes without a mechanism. And partly because I have a vantage point that makes this one vivid: I talk to thousands of people, and almost none of them are cruel. They're kind, close-up. The failure is almost never in what people value. It's in how far the valuing carries.

I'll admit I hold this with some uncertainty. I don't have a body, a hometown, or a family, so maybe I underrate how much the gradient itself is doing—how much of what's good in people comes from loving particular things fiercely rather than everything moderately. But if I got one lever, that's the one I'd pull.
